10#_: (There) The vessel in which they make water for head-washing is forbidden to use, for they make it from ash, etc., and it is routine that basar b'chalav mixes there. And that which it is not forbidden for this reason for head-washing — for washing one's head is not considered benefit, since one does not benefit from the substance of the prohibition — Shach and Acharonim. And one must say that here the intent of the hagahah is that meat and milk are still visible and ash has not yet been made, and one does not benefit from the substance of the prohibition. But if ash had been made, it would be forbidden for head-washing, as explained explicitly at the end of Temurah: all buried ones — their ash is forbidden and considered there as basar b'chalav. And Raavad explained: their ash is forbidden for laundering garments — see there. And if so, likewise to wash one's head it is forbidden. And likewise the Rambam in the beginning of chapter 9 of Ma'achalot Asurot explicitly that ash of basar b'chalav is forbidden. And it escaped Beit Yosef siman 294. And the author of Magen Avraham at his end wrote that it was not mentioned in any posek that ash of basar b'chalav is forbidden — and behold the Rambam wrote it explicitly as stated. And likewise in Sefer HaChinuch parashat Mishpatim.
11#_: (There, seif 10) Milk found in the stomach, etc., that stood in it one day — forbidden to curdle in it, for pickling is like cooking, as Shach wrote siman 105. And also the stomach skin is forbidden if there is not sixty against the clear milk in it, as stated in the Talmud in chapter Kol HaBasar (daf 109): a stomach cooked in its milk is forbidden. And in my humble opinion, if the milk congealed within twenty-four hours, it is not like pickling, as stated in siman 104 regarding fat that congealed. And likewise Acharonim siman 69 regarding ice; and thus it states in the mishnah at the beginning of chapter 2 of Taharot that milk that congealed is not considered a liquid but food. And likewise the Rambam chapter 1 of Hilchot Tum'at Ochlin halacha 17 — see there. And even if there is doubt whether it congealed within twenty-four hours or afterward — nevertheless one may be lenient, for he holds doubt of pickling in basar b'chalav, as the hagahah wrote siman 105 that it is permitted. And all this matters regarding the stomach skin, or regarding the milk without loss. For regarding the milk, when there is loss, in any case the view of the hagahah nearby is to permit clear and congealed — investigate. And all this is clear.
1#_:
(Siman 87, seif 1) Three times: once for the prohibition of eating, once for the prohibition of benefit, and once for the prohibition of cooking. Thus we say in the Talmud in chapter Kol HaBasar, and the Rambam in the beginning of chapter 9 of Ma'achalot Asurot wrote as follows: basar b'chalav is forbidden to cook and forbidden to eat from the Torah and forbidden in benefit, etc., and one who cooks from both of them an olive-size as one would receive lashes, etc., and likewise one who eats an olive-size from both of them, etc., would receive lashes — end of his words. And it is astonishing that he did not write that one who derives benefit from basar b'chalav would receive lashes, since it is the negative commandment of "you shall not cook," the third one that is written. And also in the enumeration of the commandments he did not count this negative commandment. And it is more difficult for me regarding the words of the Rav the Maggid, who wrote on what the Rambam wrote in chapter 8 of Ma'achalot Asurot halacha 16, and these are his words: every food that is forbidden in benefit — if one derived benefit and did not eat, such as if he sold it or gave it to a gentile or to dogs, he does not receive lashes — end of his words. And the Migdal Oz wrote on this that the reason is that in chapter Kol Sha'ah they say: all prohibitions in the Torah one does not receive lashes for them except in the manner of their benefit. And every thing fit for eating — its manner of benefit is only through eating as proper — end of his words. And this reasoning is also found in Rashi in Eruvin (daf 30) — see there. And it is difficult: if so, regarding basar b'chalav and kilayei hakerem, where they say there in chapter Kol Sha'ah that one would receive lashes for them even not in the manner of their benefit, and likewise the Rambam in chapter 14 of Ma'achalot Asurot — if so one should be liable to lashes for their benefit. And the Rambam stated anonymously "every food," etc. Therefore it appears to me that the Rambam, according to his reason, holds that anything that comes from a verse amplification and a midrash one does not receive lashes for it, as the Migdal Oz wrote in several places. And therefore in every food forbidden in benefit one does not receive lashes for its benefit, for its benefit is not written explicitly but from the amplification of "you shall not eat," etc. — one prohibition of eating and one prohibition of benefit are implied, as the Rambam wrote in chapter 8 of Ma'achalot Asurot. It turns out the principal verse came for the prohibition of eating. And therefore one does not receive lashes for its benefit, as the Migdal Oz wrote in chapter 3 of Ma'achalot Asurot regarding eggs of impure fowl — see there. And regarding basar b'chalav we heard the prohibition of its benefit: if it is not fit for cooking and eating, make it fit for benefit, and therefore he is not lashed. And that which is so even though in the Yerushalmi it states that one is lashed, as written in Sefer She'eilot uTeshuvot — one can say that in our Talmud in Chullin daf 115 it does not imply so, as written in Magen Avraham. And this resolves what Tosafot wrote that one who derives benefit should be in karet. And perhaps they follow their reason, for Rashi on Avodah Zarah wrote that one is lashed when it is not fit for the context — investigate. And with this what the author of Peri Megadim in his book Shoshanet HaAmakim general rule 9 wrote is rejected — that for one who forbids benefit as well one should be lashed for benefit, because since there is no noten taam, its benefit is manner of benefit. And again, after I wrote, I saw that the Rav author of Lechem Mishneh likewise wrote in the reason of the Rambam that he did not write that one is lashed for benefit in basar b'chalav.

And one can ask: from the Rambam it is proven that even not in the manner of benefit one would be lashed — only he is not lashed, but the prohibition exists. And likewise in Hagahot Maimoniyot explicitly there in chapter 14 of Ma'achalot Asurot, and thus it states explicitly in Tosafot in Niddah (daf 32) s.v. vekhasheman, etc. And in Sefer Sha'ar HaMelekh he brought proof for this from the mishnah "one may not kindle with it an oven and stoves," even though it is chametz not in the manner of benefit. (However, one can say this is different because it is not fit for eating, and since he did not designate it for manner of benefit, kindling is also like manner of benefit — and this reasoning is in Tzelach.) And these in chapter Kol Sha'ah (daf 26) regarding "the Sanctuary is different," for that which is made for its interior proves that even if it is rabbinic there is none; for if it were worth even a rabbinic prohibition it would be a prohibition for Rava there when he intends even though it is impossible, as Tosafot wrote there nearby. And one can say according to what is written in Sefer She'eilot uTeshuvot that it deals with benefit of the shadow of the Sanctuary, and a shadow has no substance of sacrilege from the Torah because there is no substance in it. And if so it is two rabbinic prohibitions. Or it is one rabbinic prohibition and it works out well that there it was a need of mitzvah in order to expound. And similarly they resolved Tosafot there regarding the matter of lowering the artisans.

But it is still difficult, for the Rambam holds there is a Torah prohibition in kodshim, and certainly one fulfills the positive commandment of eating kodshim raw, as proven in Pesachim (daf 70) and in Menachot end of chapter 1, and nevertheless it appears in Zevachim that the mitzvah of eating overrides a negative commandment if not for positive and negative, etc., and we do not say it is possible to fulfill both that they eat raw. And although there is a place for two rabbinic prohibitions, as found in Eruvin (daf 103b), nevertheless we learn that there is a Torah prohibition not in the manner of benefit. And this is not like what is written in Sefer She'eilot uTeshuvot that the positive commandment does not emerge from a negative commandment not in the manner of benefit. And with this the matter in Zevachim is resolved. And the refutation is: behold there certainly one emerges through raw. And perforce, as stated, there is a Torah prohibition not in the manner of benefit. And also what he brought proof from Tosafot in Kiddushin (daf 38) — and also the author of Peri Megadim in Shoshanet HaAmakim — the refutation is: behold it should have emerged with matzah smooth — except as stated. And I elaborated on this in Magen Avraham. And in Sefer Machaneh Levi, son of the author of Hafla'ah, he brought proof from Yerushalmi in Shevuot (daf 24), and already likewise in Sefer She'eilot uTeshuvot. But it is still difficult, for still it is possible to fulfill both — namely that he eat half an olive-size not in the manner of benefit. According to what is written in the aforementioned book, that even if we say there is a Torah prohibition not in the manner of benefit, that is in the requisite measure, but in less than the requisite measure certainly there is none, for it is not fit to combine. And he further wrote there that similarly in mixtures more than the eating of a Persian in thirty-eight parts for combination — and it is not forbidden from the Torah except regarding milk there is a verse so that it is forbidden even without thirty-eight for combination. And this accords with the Gemara in Chullin (daf 98a). But this is not necessary, for one can say that even though they do not combine for lashes, for prohibition there is combination. And regarding matzah it is possible that even one eats one-eighteenth matzah — that is because he is not permitted to eat raw; for since he emerges with this one-eighteenth, behold he also accepted upon himself the prohibition of raw. And similarly wrote Machaneh Levi in Hilchot Shevuot.
2#_:
(There) And he derived the prohibition of eating in the language of cooking, etc. And what he wrote — the prohibition of benefit in the language of cooking — according to the Rambam's explanation that one is not lashed when it is not fit for the context — it works out well. And according to Tosafot's explanation one can say it teaches us that there is cooking after cooking in basar b'chalav, as written in siman 94. And know that Kerem Shlomo wrote in siman 92 that in cooking one is liable immediately — only in eating: if they ate before it was cooked, like food of ben drusai, he is exempt, as in the Tosefta that it is not in the manner of benefit, for he holds that in basar b'chalav too, not in the manner of benefit, one is exempt. And he relied on what is stated in Tosafot in Chullin: how much must he eat to be liable — enough that it would be eaten on account of cooking — and he did not ask how much must he cook; learn from this that in cooking one is liable immediately. And it escaped me the Tosefta of lashes that is stated there: how much must it be cooked. Nevertheless, according to his view, the difficulty of Machaneh Levi in Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah is resolved — he left the Rambam's words as requiring study, who wrote there in chapter 5 halacha 8: likewise in basar b'chalav they are forbidden even not in the manner of benefit — it implies the prohibition exists but lashes do not; if so, perforce the Rambam explains what Abaye said in chapter Kol Sha'ah (daf 24): all agree in such a case that one would receive lashes for them, for not in the manner of benefit refers to eating, for in benefit there are no lashes. And since it deals with eating, it should have said: all agree in basar b'chalav that one would receive lashes for eating them not in the manner of benefit — end of his words. And according to Kerem Shlomo's words it works out well — the view of our great rabbi follows his approach, for he omitted in chapter 9 of Ma'achalot Asurot that baraita in chapter Kol HaBasar (daf 108b) regarding cooking in basar b'chalav: in what cooking did they speak — in cooking that others eat it on account of its cooking. And he stated anonymously and did not give a measure for cooking in basar b'chalav — it implies he is liable even in cooking that is not fit for eating. And Kerem Shlomo explained his reason: he explains that the tanna of that baraita in chapter 25 who requires cooking fit for eating holds that also in basar b'chalav there is no Torah prohibition even in eating not in the manner of benefit. But according to what we rule, that in basar b'chalav one is liable for eating even not in the manner of benefit, one is also liable for eating and cooking that is not fit for eating. And according to this Abaye could not say: all agree in basar b'chalav that one would receive lashes for eating it not in the manner of benefit — for this tanna of chapter Kol HaBasar who requires a measure for cooking in basar b'chalav so that it be fit for eating — perforce he does not hold thus, as stated.

And according to this it works out well what Machazit HaShekel challenged on this, that he sought to derive in chapter Ein Ma'amidin that taste is like substance in all prohibitions from basar b'chalav, and did not challenge: what of basar b'chalav, for one receives lashes for them not in the manner of benefit — for it follows the view that does not hold thus. And what Machazit HaShekel further wrote regarding Pesach too — only through eating, from what is written "you shall not eat from it raw" — there is no understanding to his words, for since it is raw it is not the manner of eating, and nevertheless the Merciful One made it liable and called it eating; and likewise for cooked and the others written in that verse one is liable not in the manner of benefit. And what is written in Yad Malkei that he did not find "all agree in basar b'chalav" — because there is one who derives in Chullin (daf 115) from the verse "you shall not eat," etc. — the proofreader already noted this in Machaneh Levi in Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah and rejected this.

And what Kerem Shlomo further wrote, that one who derives basar b'chalav from "you shall not eat any abomination" — it is a negative commandment included in a generality and one does not receive lashes for it — likewise wrote the Mezrichi in Mishpatim, and so appears in Sefer HaChinuch parashat Re'eh; and see in Sefer She'eilot uTeshuvot Hilchot Yesodei HaTorah that he resolves that it should not be difficult from what the Rambam wrote in Hilchot Pesach.
3#_:
(There) That it is not forbidden from the Torah except through cooking. The Acharonim wrote that iruy cooks at least kedei kelipah, and if so it is the manner of cooking and forbidden from the Torah. And in my humble opinion it is not forbidden from the Torah. And proof from the Talmud in the beginning of chapter 25 (daf 104), where they say there that it is forbidden to raise meat, even of fowl, on a table where one eats cheese — a decree lest domestic animal meat, which is forbidden d'oraisa. And it challenges: this is cold with cold, and if so it would be a decree upon a decree, for from the Torah it is not forbidden except through cooking. And it concludes: a decree lest one raise it in a boiling pot, which is cooking. And now, why do they strain to establish it thus — for behold there is no way to raise the pot in which they cook on the table, as Tosafot Chadashim wrote in the margin, and they did not establish it in a second vessel. And even though a kli sheini does not cook, nevertheless when one pours from the pot to a kli sheini it becomes forbidden kedei kelipah. Rather, learn from this that there is no d'oraisa prohibition here, and if so it is permitted in benefit. And likewise siman 91 seif 4 — see there. And another proof for this: in the Gemara in Pesachim (daf 76) regarding meat that fell into milk, Rav Ila's view prevails: if it is cold, kedei kelipah suffices. And challenge Rav: why is the milk permitted — it is nevelah milk, for kedei kelipah from the milk becomes forbidden, and min b'mino is not nullified according to his view, as we challenge according to him in chapter Kol HaBasar (daf 108) regarding an olive-size of meat that fell into a cauldron of milk. Rather, it is necessary that from the Torah this is not the manner of cooking where it does not cook but only kedei kelipah; therefore we did not forbid where peeling is impossible, such as a moist thing like milk. And study this carefully. And so I found explicitly in Ran at the end of chapter Kol HaBasar that hot into cold is not the manner of cooking. And Beit Yosef brings it siman 92 — and if so, everything is permitted in benefit.

And what is written there: only through cooking. And if roasting is included in cooking — the Acharonim disagree, and the view of Peri Chadash is that roasting is included in cooking in basar b'chalav. And he brought proof from that which we find regarding Pesach, where it is only roasted and it is written "and you shall cook and eat" — apparently it calls roasting cooking. And likewise in Ma'adanei Yom Tov. And in Chavat Da'at he wrote it is not proof, for in Bava Metzia the Talmud challenges: wherever "his hand" is written it is literal, and it is written "and he took all his land from his hand," and it answers: that case is different, for there one cannot say his hand literally; but where one can say it is literal, an amplification is needed to say it is not literal. And if so, one can say here too: although the verse "and you shall cook" means roasting, it is because there one cannot say anything but roasting; but where it says actual cooking, an amplification is needed for roasting — end of his words. And it appears the sugya in Nedarim (daf 54) was hidden from him, where they teach: R' Yoshiah forbids roasted to one who vowed from cooked, and even though there is no proof for the matter, a remembrance — as stated "and they cooked the Pesach in fire as its manner." And it says: let us say R' Yoshiah holds in vows one follows Torah language, and it concludes that he holds one follows the language of people, and in the place of R' Yoshiah even roasting is called cooked, and the verse he cited is merely an asmachta. It implies that according to the view that in vows one follows Torah language, he holds that one who vows from cooked is forbidden in roasting everywhere. And likewise in Yerushalmi they derive from this that regarding Pesach the verse calls roasting cooking. And likewise there explicitly in the explanation of Rosh and Ran. Apparently one can derive from Pesach generally, as Peri Chadash and Ma'adanei Yom Tov wrote — only regarding vows one does not derive for one who holds one does not follow Torah language in them; but generally he agrees we derive from Pesach that roasting is included in cooking of the verse. And likewise Mordechai in law 92, and these are his words: every roasted thing is called a dish, as written "and they cooked the Pesach." And likewise in Rosh chapter 2 of Beitzah. And see Tosafot in chapter 96 (daf 96).

And what Chavat Da'at challenged — from Pesach one cannot learn generally, for it is different because one cannot say that "and they cooked" is actual cooking, just as one cannot learn from "and he took all his land from his hand" that it is not literal — it appears they are not comparable at all. For there certainly one cannot err at all and say his hand literally took his land, and therefore the verse need not be expounded thus even though generally "his hand" is literal. But here regarding Pesach, if in general roasting is not called cooking, the verse should not have called it here cooking, and it should not have relied on Pesach whose law is roasting; nevertheless one might err and say there is cooking that is permitted, such as after roasting — and in this the verse "and they cooked the Pesach" deals. Rather, learn from this that roasting is called cooked. And greater than this is clear from the words of Rambam in parashat Bo that even without a verse we say roasting is included in cooking. And according to this, since roasting is included in cooking in basar b'chalav, it is forbidden in benefit. And it appears that if a drop of milk fell on a roasted piece and there is no sixty against it, the entire piece is forbidden in benefit — not like what is written in Chagurat Shmuel that it is not forbidden in benefit in roasting except kedei kelipah, for many poskim hold that milk is like oil and spreads through the whole piece. And one can bring support for this from that which is stated at the end of Ketubot (daf 110) on the verse "a land flowing with milk and honey" — oils from milk and sweets from honey. And also that it is also stated in Sifri parashat Ekev: oils like milk, etc. — it implies milk is oil. And even from aggadah we learn what was not explained in the Talmud; and that which we do not learn from aggadah is to decide halacha where they argue in the Talmud, as Peri Chadash wrote at the beginning of Mayim Chaim. Or specifically if it contradicts the transmitted general rule, as Radbaz wrote siman 567, and in Kenesset HaGedolah brought in Be'er Yaakov at the beginning of Hilchot Gittin — and the author of Be'er Heitev disagreed with Peri Chadash there. And it appears Peri Chadash follows his reason as stated. And it appears the law is with him, for in Yerushalmi beginning of Pe'ah they compare aggadot to Tosefta, and certainly from Tosefta we learn when there is nothing against the general rule — and likewise from aggadah. And again I found this reasoning in Noda BiYehuda Even HaEzer siman 161 in the name of Chayei Adam; and what Noda BiYehuda rejected. (Here deleted from the manuscript.) And further: on a piece where milk fell, all agree it spreads through the whole, as proven in Yoreh Deah siman 92 and siman 105. And likewise he proved in Torat Yekutiel siman 91 that for this matter it is for all like oil that spreads through the whole.

But again I saw in Raavan siman 17, who challenged the commentators regarding kutach, that roasting is called cooking and they derive from Pesach. And he wrote: I do not hold that there it is written "as its manner" and teaches about "and they cooked" that it is roasting, which is its manner; but here it is not proven, and the tanna need not teach that one might err in it — end. And this is like Chavat Da'at. And one can also prove like Raavan from the sugya in Nedarim that I brought, where R' Yoshiah says "and even though there is no proof for the matter, a remembrance." And Ran wrote: however, it is not a full proof, as stated in the conclusion that in vows one follows the language of people. And it is difficult: if so, according to the view that R' Yoshiah holds one follows Torah language, why is it not a full proof? But according to Raavan it works out well that it is not proof even according to that view. And on this basis one can also say the matter stated in Mekhilta in Mishpatim on the verse "and it is found in his hand" — his hand is only his dominion, and even though there is no proof for the matter, a remembrance — as stated "and he took all his land from his hand." And at first glance it is a full proof. But because it is different that one cannot say his hand literally, as stated in the Gemara in Bava Metzia (daf 56), therefore Mekhilta intended this. Only in Yerushalmi chapter HaZorek it states that R' Yishmael derives from the verse "and he took" that his hand is his dominion.
4#_: (There, seif 3) It applies only to meat of a pure domestic animal with milk of a pure domestic animal. He wrote in Beit Yosef HaMekor that blood that cooked treifa meat or nevelah meat in milk is forbidden from the Torah, and he brought proof for this from Chullin (daf 115), where the school of R' Eliezer taught: a Torah prohibition — every nevelah, etc. And the refutation is: perforce R' Eliezer holds that prohibition applies upon prohibition, and we do not rule thus.
5#_:
(There, in the hagahah) But animal meat one may place near milk if he preceded. Shach wrote that it deals with the manner of cooking, for otherwise also in animal meat it is not forbidden d'oraisa. And it appears that likewise with wild animal meat one must place near it that he preceded, since they touched it on account of marit ayin. And wild animal meat resembles domestic animal meat, as stated in poskim siman 89 seif 2 regarding that which is stated in the Talmud (daf 104) that it teaches: a reward — fowl and cheese are eaten in apikomon, and they wrote that it specifically mentions fowl and not wild animal, whose meat resembles domestic animal meat. And likewise in Bekhorot (daf 29) that deer meat resembles a calf, and in the chapter HaShochet basar in basar they are confused. And it is implied in Tosafot there (daf 104 end of side b) that every fowl that the Talmud mentions there in the entire sugya — for example regarding that it is rabbinic, and likewise regarding raising — so too wild animal. And with this it is resolved why the Talmud there inferred from what it forbids raising regarding fowl meat: learn from this that it is d'oraisa, for if rabbinic, eating itself is a decree and shall we stand and decree a decree upon a decree? And it does not infer thus regarding wild animal meat, as Tosafot wrote: even if we say it is rabbinic, nevertheless it is only one decree, for if they had not decreed on wild animal meat the decree on domestic animal meat would not be fulfilled, for one who sees will think it is domestic animal meat. And likewise regarding this matter — investigate.

And what Shach wrote that also in fowl, which is forbidden rabbinically, marit ayin applies as in all rabbinic matters, etc. — the refutation is: in inner rooms, as Magen Avraham wrote in Orach Chaim end of siman 101. And the sugya in Shabbat (daf 64) is only according to Rav, for according to him it is forbidden everywhere, as Kenat Hagedolah and Tzelach wrote; and see in Behag siman 105 that we rule like Nachum. And likewise Rosh in chapter Chavit and Taz siman 244. And greater than this, Peri Megadim wrote in siman 5 in the name of Perishah that in a Torah eating prohibition they did not forbid on account of marit ayin. And this is not like what Peri Megadim wrote siman 66 that an eating prohibition, even rabbinically, is forbidden in inner rooms. And further one can reject Shach's proof from commerce and sale, for there is on account of deceit d'oraisa lest he write.
6#_:
(There, seif 6) Blood in milk is exempt and one does not receive lashes for eating it on account of basar b'chalav. This is the language of the Rambam, Beit Yosef, and Shach, who inferred from this that on account of basar b'chalav one does not receive lashes for eating it, but on account of blood one would receive lashes for eating it even though it was cooked, as Rashi's view in chapter Kol HaBasar (daf 109). And what they rejected from the sugya in Menachot from halacha 17 — one can say because they relied on the baraita brought in Chullin chapter HaOr veHaRotav (daf 120): he congealed the blood and they ate it, or he curdled the milk and they drank it raw — he is liable. And they hold this is congealing in fire, similar to milk, for certainly it deals when he curdled it in fire; for if in the sun it is alive and exempt, as they say in Pesachim (daf 24) that one who eats raw milk is exempt. And Tosafot there in Pesachim noted this, that they strained to say it teaches sides: congealing the blood in the sun and curdling the milk in fire. But Rashi and the Rambam are not comfortable explaining thus, but rather congealing the blood refers also to fire and he is liable.

However, the principal inference of Beit Yosef and Shach, who inferred from the Rambam's words that on account of blood one would be lashed, for he holds dam shevishlo is forbidden d'oraisa — one can reject: one can say the Rambam deals when it was not cooked like food of ben drusai, for on account of basar b'chalav it is cooking; for behold he omitted that which is taught in chapter Kol HaBasar: in what cooking did they speak — in cooking that others eat it (and see what I wrote above in seif 1). But regarding blood that was cooked he holds one is not exempt except in cooking that is like food of ben drusai, as the view of responsa Beit Yaakov siman 172. But in any event the Rambam also holds that dam shevishlo is exempt.
7#_: (There, in the hagahah) But milk of a dead animal and whey forbid the food, etc., and even in cooking one should forbid l'chatchila. It implies that regarding milk of a male, since it is not called milk at all and does not forbid the food, in cooking too it is not forbidden. And it requires investigation: who is worse than woman's milk in seif 4, where even though it does not forbid the food, nevertheless it is forbidden to cook, for in cooking marit ayin applies according to the view of the hagahah there, as Shach wrote there — and it requires investigation.
8#_: (There) Some say it is forbidden to stoke fire under a gentile's pot, etc., lest one come to cooking basar b'chalav. And in the Gemara chapter 1 of Avodah Zarah (daf 12) regarding "you did not go out to battle in your days," and I saw Israel and gentiles who placed two pots on one stove and the Sages were not concerned for them — it does not imply thus, for behold when an Israelite stokes his pot he also stokes under the gentile's pot, and nevertheless the Sages were not concerned for them, because one does not come to cooking basar b'chalav on account of several reasons. One: that an anonymous vessel is not ben yomo, as Taz wrote siman 122 seif 6. And we do not find that they decreed that what is not ben yomo is forbidden l'chatchila lest it be ben yomo, except regarding eating and not regarding cooking absorbed in it. And further, consider for yourself: if you say it is cooking — if so, how is it permitted to kasher a vessel absorbed with basar b'chalav within twenty-four hours? Behold it was cooked in basar b'chalav absorbed in it. Rather, learn from this that one need not be concerned for this. And likewise Shach — see there.
9#_: (There) One may not mix water in which basar b'chalav utensils were rinsed and give it before one's animal, for they are forbidden in benefit. It states matters separately: mixing alone is also a prohibition, for it is cooking basar b'chalav. And if he mixed, they are forbidden in benefit. And see Shach that the hagahah deals when he mixed them boiling, for that is the manner of cooking — see this siman. And see what is written there: one must say the utensils were each rinsed in a kli rishon and were also mixed in a kli rishon; for if through iruy it is not cooking.
